newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-INDIANS DEAL LOFTON TO BRAVES FOR GRISSOM, JUSTICE.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-INDIANS DEAL LOFTON TO BRAVES FOR GRISSOM, JUSTICE.

text.p: The teams that faced off in the 1995 World Series pulled the trigger on a blockbuster trade Tuesday, with three All-Stars switching uniforms one week before the start of the 1997 season.
The Cleveland Indians sent centerfielder Kenny Lofton and relief pitcher Alan Embree to the Atlanta Braves for outfielders Marquis Grissom and David Justice.

The Braves acquired the premier leadoff batter in baseball in Lofton, while saving salary money which they can use to help retain four-time Cy Young Award winner Greg Maddux next season by shipping out Justice and Grissom.
The Indians picked up another fine leadoff man and fielder in Grissom, and from Justice some of the home run power they lost when Albert Belle signed with the Chicago White Sox.

"It's like somebody stabbed me in the back...it's tough, it's really tough," complained a distraught Lofton, an All-Star the past three years who said he thought he might finish his career with Cleveland.

The Indians felt they got a different message from the speedy centerfielder, who becomes eligible for free agency after the upcoming season, when he turned down a multi-year offer and announced he would not conduct contract negotiations during the season.

"Kenny Lofton made it very clear that he wanted to go out onto the market, and the Cleveland Indians were not prepared to allow that to happen and come up with nothing, so we took a very proactive stance and made what we consider to be a very good baseball trade," said Indians general manager John Hart.

The 29-year-old Lofton led the American League in stolen bases each of the last five years. He is a career .313 hitter and a four-time Gold Glove winner, who enjoyed a career-best year last season, hitting .317 with 14 homers, 67 RBI, 132 runs scored and 75 stolen bases in 154 games last year.

"This very significant deal brings us arguably the game's finest centre fielder and leadoff hitter in Kenny Lofton," said Braves general manager John Schuerholz. "In addition, our bullpen is strengthened considerably by the acquisition of hard-throwing lefthander Alan Embree."
Grissom will immediately step in for Lofton at leadoff and centerfield. The two-time All-Star and four-time Golden Glove winner twice led the National League in steals when he was with Montreal.
The 29-year-old Grissom has a career .281 batting average with 89 homers, 392 RBI and 323 stolen bases in 995 games. He hit .308 with 23 homers, 74 RBI and 28 steals last season.
"It's a business, I realised that when I went through arbitration a couple of years ago," Grissom said from the Braves' spring training facility in West Palm Beach, Florida.
"I just want to focus my time and attention now to getting used to the American League."

Justice is also a two-time All-Star. But the Braves had been seeking to unload his salary since the end last season. He has two years left at $12.5 million on his original five-year, $28 million deal. Grissom signed a four-year, $19.2 million deal with the Braves in 1996.
Justice, 31, was the National League Rookie of the Year for Atlanta in 1990 and helped them to their lone World Series win over Cleveland in 1995.
His 1996 season was cut short due to shoulder surgery after playing in just 40 games. Justice was hitting .321 before suffering a dislocation of his shoulder.
"The two players we're receiving are very talented players," said Indians manager Mike Hargrove. "In my mind we are a much better ballclub at this time today than we were at this time yesterday."

The left-handed hitting Justice enjoyed his best season in 1993 when he had 40 homers and 120 RBI. He has 160 homers, 522 RBI and a .275 batting average in 817 games over eight seasons with the Braves.
Embree made just 24 appearances for the Indians last season and was 1-1 with a 6.39 ERA in 31 innings. He limited left-handed hitters to a .186 batting average (8-for-43).
